Although cute at first, novelty accounts can ultimately overwhelm otherwise meaningful exchanges and creativity.

I propose that Voat adopt an official policy in order to mitigate the impact of "fedora-style" comments, trolling, and posts.

Questions/Concerns:

If we restrict novelty accounts altogether, is this too much of a detriment to expression?

If novelty accounts become popular, what's to stop ridiculous comment threads?

Are some kinds of novelty accounts acceptable? Is this simply part of evolving "meme culture"?

What other way could we possibly address this before it becomes an issue?
I agree that useless accounts suck, but some 'novelty' accounts are actually alright, like reddit's /u/AWildSketchAppeared.
That's what makes this a challenging issue. One could definitely make a case that /u/AWildSketchAppeared contributes to the discussion and creativity of a thread.

Personally I would be against that restriction. Most o us are here to get away from people who want to impose too many rules for their own connivence. I have no problem with folks having a good time with the novelty accounts, even if it's not my cup of tea.
I totally get where you're coming from, and you make a valid point. That said, I think we have a unique opportunity to learn from some of the issues that lead to cheapening "that other place".
Agreed. Lots of folks are here because the other place is changing the rules. And now they're here trying to make new rules.
Exactly. We're given our own tools (downvotes, ignore), that's all that's needed to solve the 'problem', if you see this as one.

Some novelty accounts that come with good content would be nice though. I know that one such account from reddit, who writes music, considered joining voat. And it would be fun if one of those "here I drew your username/comment" appeared as well. So like, not so much meme accounts as accounts that do creative things.
Perhaps we could draw a distinction between creative/fictional accounts and more juvenile/troll-y accounts?
That sounds like a good idea. A lot of people love the more creative ones (since they're awesome). The other accounts are more.. yeah..
Why is it that I read all of your comments in the form of yelling?

I would not support this. I think if you don't like a comment and think it's not a good contribution then you should downvote it. One of the draws of voat is less censorship, more freedom of speech. Let's not ruin that by trying to get things banned that annoy us.

The challenge as I see it: if/when Voat becomes a popular destination on the internet, it could potentially fall victim to mediocrity if we don't have a reasonable foundation in place to address those looking simply to score points, rather than contribute.

Maybe some sort of classification, and options for posts to turn them off (perhaps even to the level of threads) I'm kinda new to this sort of social media, so I am not really in full-contact with the terminologies used here. ^^;
That's a good idea! If there was a "novelty tag" that allowed filtering... something to consider. Although I'm not sure on the logistics.
I prefer lawlessness. I miss the old old old internet

I say allow them all, lest we begin the dangerous trek down the road of silencing speech and/or personas we don't particularly care for. Why not let the content of said accounts speak for itself and up/downvoat accordingly? Also, what would be the logic underlying such rules, other than that @writtenloudly thinks you shouldn't be allowed to comment/post because he doesn't like it?

Personally, I think that keeping the up/downvoat counter next to the post and removing the "sort by best/top" feature for comments would be a good thing. Sure, you'd have to sort through more comments than you're used to, and some are bound to be inflammatory, trolling, SJW stuff, fedora-related literature and probably a million other points of view you might not like, but so what? At least no one would be silenced by merely being "downvoted to oblivion". Truthfully, I really have no idea if this would actually be a good idea or how to even begin properly managing a diverse internet community, so who knows?

Perhaps at a later date when things are more stable, we could introduce a RES-style tagging system that would allow users to mark trolls/spammers/people literally worse than Hitler or something. Also, I haven't figured the whole place out yet, but an "ignore user" button would be fantastic to edit out the obvious spammers/novelty accounts we personally don't like.

My point of view is for absolute freedom of speech barring the obvious illegal material such as child porn, etc.

I would also put DOXing in a separate category labeled as "courtesy". While it isn't technically illegal to share public information about another user, we'd all probably prefer that it didn't happen, so as a community we'll agree that it's breaking the rules and not allow it. Again, I could be wrong, some people might be ok with that sort of thing.

Everybody should have a voice, even if you're a jackass, or running a once-funny joke into the ground, or white-knighting, or trolling the absolute crap out of everybody else. That's what makes the internet great.

I definitely agree with you on a lot of these points, @MaxTrollbot . I'm not certain whether adopting a policy on novelty accounts is a good idea, or even necessarily feasible--but it does seem like something that the Voat community should spend some time thinking about--hence this post.

It's not that I personally don't like novelty accounts, but I noticed that the decline in the overall quality of content posted on "that other site" seemed to correlate with the rise of excessive novelty accounts. All online communities adopt at least some rules/regulations/guidelines. I suppose one way of looking at this, would be to consider what kind of Voat culture we'd like to foster.

I've been exposed to linux a few times in the past, but I've had to start using it a lot for work recently, and I'm starting to appreciate some of its features and differences from Windows. I was curious why people seemed so invested in the terminal, and was directed to "The Art of Programming in Unix", which I've started reading.

One thing that stood out to me with the book was the "Things that Unix does right/wrong" sections, and the general points for why Linux is better than existing GUI-based systems. I've grown up using entirely GUI systems, but I can definitely see the inherent value in having a command-line interface available. Still, I find myself wanting some GUI-based features a lot of the time, particularly when trying to navigate file structures or affect a specific set of files, for instance. I see a real void space where a terminal can't easily select an arbitrary list of non-similar files (tab-completion is the best you'll get), and a GUI can't do much with said list.

With all that said, I'm wondering if there exists a kind of hybrid - a Linux-based graphical OS that integrates the terminal's functionality well. I know there are GUI-based Linux distros, but they only really offer the terminal in the same way Windows offers the command line, at least in my experience.
I'm envisioning each window having a terminal box somewhere that simply holds a command, and allows you to apply it on selected items in the window (maybe with a pipe, maybe as some kind of identifier). I imagine each window would also have an identifier somewhere on itself so you could interface between windows (e.g. copy files while renaming by selecting the files, copy to other window open in target destination, and target them with a regex). Naturally the window would be built out of smaller parts, so the default would feature the header bar (max/min, close etc.), a terminal box, a file viewer, and a filesystem browser clamped on the side. The idea here being to make it easy to build a custom window with a simple definition - perhaps you customise the default to show a preview of a selected file using less on the right. I imagine this modular design could easily be applied to the desktop too, such that if you desired, you could easily split it 50/50 with the GUI and a terminal.

I have not had much sleep and its been a long day. I don't know if what I said makes sense, or sounds useful, but it was something I was thinking of today. I'd like to hear ideas from people with a lot more experience here than I, because there's always the possibility that the gap between terminal and GUI can be bridged in a much better way. "Distrust all claims for one true way" of course.

You said you're new to Linux, and what you suggest is not a terrible idea, but there are existing things to do what you want. You don't know them yet.

Maybe you might want to learn how to do things the *NIX way?

It is a contrived example, mostly for brevity. I know I've had situations like it in the past, but can't recall them, as is often the case. I suppose a recent example that sort of fits is a situation I had at work. I was configuring some tests for a shoutcast server, where we were testing roughly 20 stations/ports. We wanted a certain number of them to run 1500 connections, and a certain number to run only 600, which meant specifying a variable in the script. If we want to up the connections on some specific stations, using either the terminal or a GUI we'd have to manually select each one and replace that value (unless it coincided precisely with all the ones with a specific number of connections). Ultimately this isn't a big deal for 20 shell scripts, but considering we have about 60 possible ports to test, if we ever wanted to do a larger-scale test and distribute it across all the ports with more varying numbers, it would be a right pain. The easiest option at that point would be to delete and re-generate the scripts.
I'm sure there are ways to do these things in the terminal, just as there are ways to do most things in a GUI - it's just a little more painful than it necessarily has to be. As a programmer, I'm quite happy and eager to learn the *NIX way, but as a designer and a user, I'm also eager to make it more efficient and accessible - I imagine many people would be more interested in learning *NIX if they were presented with "Windows, but like way more powerful" (and incidentally with less abstractions too!).

Honestly, I think the only thing I would need in this regard is a means of simply dragging and dropping files/directories into the terminal. I'm new to Linux, too, and I always thought that would be a nice feature. Not even sure, it might exist.
In most Linux distributions I've used, you can drag files and directories from the graphical file manager into a terminal window, and it will insert the paths to each selected item into the prompt.
I think I'm stupid enough that I may have never tried it...

It's not the kind of thing you tend to do usually so it's easy to miss the feature. Either you're working in a terminal and typing commands or you're manipulating the GUI with the mouse, but if you're doing the former, it breaks your workflow to grab the mouse to drag and drop files into your terminal. It's often easier to just type the file-names in and use tab-completion, or use wildcards or grep to search for the patterns you need.
